prompt: What distinguishes inner-sphere from outer-sphere electron transfer?

choices.text: In inner-sphere transfer, the redox partners are bound together through a shared ligand; in outer-sphere transfer, the electron moves between species that are close but not bound to each other
In outer-sphere transfer, the redox partners are bound together through a shared ligand; in inner-sphere transfer, they are only close to each other
choices.why: This is reversed. Sharing a ligand puts the partner in the metal's inner sphere, so that is inner-sphere transfer.

choices.text: Inner-sphere transfer moves the metal's d electrons, while outer-sphere transfer moves only ligand electrons
choices.why: The labels describe whether the partners are bound together or merely nearby, not which electrons move.

choices.text: In outer-sphere transfer, the two metals must collide and exchange ligands
choices.why: In outer-sphere transfer, the two metals react without ever getting into each other's coordination spheres.

explanation: If the redox partner is bound within the metal ion's inner sphere, for example through a ligand shared by the two metals, the reaction is an inner-sphere electron transfer. When electrons move between species that are close but not bound to one another, it is an outer-sphere transfer: the electron travels through space, a distance generally limited to a few angstroms, and the farther apart the metals, the less likely the reaction.

prompt: In the qualitative picture of Marcus theory, what is the main barrier to outer-sphere electron transfer?

choices.text: Reorganizing bond lengths, bond angles and solvent around the metals
The time the electron needs to travel between the metals
choices.why: The electron is small and very fast. The barrier has little to do with its motion and everything to do with the slow-moving atoms.

choices.text: Breaking a bridging bond between the two metals
choices.why: Outer-sphere transfer has no bridge; the metals never enter each other's coordination spheres.

choices.text: The need for the reduction potential to be zero
choices.why: Reactions with nonzero reduction potentials transfer electrons too, and even a zero-potential self-exchange has a barrier. The barrier comes from reorganization.

explanation: An electron is small and very fast, while the atoms around it are big, heavy and slow. The barrier comes from reorganizing those atoms: bond vibrations in the coordination sphere (bond lengths and angles) and solvent molecules outside it. For example, iron(II) and iron(III) complexes have very different bond distances, so right after an electron hops, both irons would sit in sub-optimal coordination environments.

prompt: In the Marcus picture, when do the reorganizations of bonds and solvent happen relative to the electron's jump?

choices.text: Before the jump, through random molecular motions; the electron then moves almost instantly
After the jump, as the products relax to their new optimum geometry
choices.why: Because the electron moves so rapidly, the reorganizations are thought to happen before the transfer, through random motions.

choices.text: During the jump, with the moving electron dragging the ligands along
choices.why: The electron moves so fast that it reaches the other atom before anything else has a chance to move.

choices.text: Never; the ligands and solvent keep their original positions throughout
choices.why: Bond lengths, angles and solvent positions must change, and that cost in energy is what creates the barrier.

explanation: The reorganizations, involving solvent molecules, bond lengths, coordination geometry and so on, are thought to occur before electron transfer, via random motions of the molecules. Once they have happened, nothing holds the electron back, and its motion is so rapid that it ends up on the other atom before anything moves again. The barrier is the energy needed for the heavy atoms to reach a set of coordinates accessible both before and after the transfer.

prompt: In a self-exchange reaction, an electron passes from an iron(II) complex to an otherwise identical iron(III) complex, so the two states have the same energy. Does this reaction have an activation barrier?

choices.text: Yes; the reduction potential is zero, but the coordination and solvation environments still have to reorganize
No; with a reduction potential of zero there is no barrier
choices.why: Zero driving force removes the energy difference between the states, not the barrier. Fe(II) and Fe(III) have different bond lengths, so reorganization is still needed.

choices.text: No; reactant and product are the same, so nothing has to change
choices.why: The two irons switch oxidation states, and the Fe(III) complex has shorter bonds than the Fe(II) complex. Each complex must reorganize.

choices.text: Yes; the barrier comes from a large negative free energy change
choices.why: In a self-exchange the free energy change is zero. The barrier comes entirely from reorganization.

explanation: When an electron moves between two metals of the same kind, the two states have the same energy and the reduction potential is zero. But the Fe(III) complex has shorter bonds than the Fe(II) complex, because of its greater electrostatic interaction with the ligands, and the solvent must adjust too. These reorganizations pose a major barrier to the reaction even though nothing new forms.

prompt: According to the section, how would replacing the water between two redox partners with a less polar solvent likely affect outer-sphere electron transfer?

choices.text: It would slow the transfer, because a less polar solvent is less able to stabilize the ions
It would speed up the transfer, because a less polar solvent stabilizes the ions better
choices.why: This is reversed. The section says a less polar solvent is less able to stabilize ions, so it expects slower transfer.

choices.text: It would have no effect, because the solvent lies outside the coordination sphere
choices.why: Solvent reorganization outside the coordination sphere is part of the barrier, and ion stability depends heavily on the surrounding medium.

choices.text: It would stop the transfer completely, because only water molecules can reorganize
choices.why: Adjustments happen in non-polar solvents too, through weaker forces such as ion–induced dipole interactions.

explanation: This is the section's answer to its own exercise. As charge moves, water molecules shift or pivot, presenting their negative ends to the more positive ion, to stabilize the ions. A less polar solvent would be less able to stabilize ions, so the electron would be slower to transfer; it would also be a poorer medium for transmitting an electron, which is charged and stabilized by polar solvents. Similar adjustments still happen in non-polar solvents, but through weaker interactions such as ion–induced dipole forces.

prompt: For a series of cobalt oxidants, the electron transfer rate constant rises from 3.0 M^−1 s^−1 at E° = 0.12 V to 6000 M^−1 s^−1 at E° = 0.60 V. How does the Marcus picture explain this trend?

choices.text: A more negative ΔG lowers the crossing point of the two energy surfaces, so the barrier falls
A more positive reduction potential raises the barrier, but the electron moves faster
choices.why: The barrier decreases as the product surface slides down. The electron's speed is not what limits the rate.

choices.text: Kinetics always tracks thermodynamics, so the rate keeps rising as E° increases
choices.why: The section warns that kinetics doesn't always track thermodynamics. At very large driving forces, Marcus theory predicts the inverted region, where rates fall.

choices.text: A more positive reduction potential shortens the distance between the metals
choices.why: The reduction potential shifts the energy of the product state; it doesn't move the reactants closer together.

explanation: A positive reduction potential (a negative free energy change) slides the energy surface of the product state downward, so the intersection point of the two surfaces, where the electron can pass from one state to the other, also slides down. The barrier decreases: the more exothermic the reaction, the lower its barrier. The cobalt data agree, with the rate rising dramatically as E° becomes more positive.

prompt: In a series of cobalt oxidants, Co(EDTA) (E° = 0.60 V) reacts with k = 6000 M^−1 s^−1 and [Co(diene)(NH3)2]^3+ (E° = 0.12 V) with k = 3.0 M^−1 s^−1. By what factor is the Co(EDTA) reaction faster?
explanation: 6000 ÷ 3.0 = 2000. An increase of 0.48 V in reduction potential gives a rate constant about 2000 times larger. A plot of k against E° for the series is not linear; it becomes more linear with a log scale on the y axis, so the relationship looks closer to exponential.

prompt: What does Marcus theory predict for the rate of electron transfer as a reaction becomes extremely exergonic?

choices.text: The rate passes through a maximum and then decreases as the barrier grows again: the Marcus inverted region
The rate keeps increasing without limit
choices.why: Marcus predicted that past some point the barrier gets higher and reactions slow down.

choices.text: The rate reaches a maximum and holds steady at that plateau
choices.why: The section is explicit: reactions don't just level off; the barrier gets higher and higher and the reactions slower and slower.

choices.text: The rate falls as soon as the free energy change becomes negative
choices.why: Over the normal range, a more negative free energy change speeds the reaction. The slowdown comes only at very large driving forces.

explanation: As the reduction potential becomes ever more positive, the barrier first falls, but past some point it gets higher and higher and the reactions get slower. Nobody had observed this when Marcus predicted it. Later, Miller's data (1984) showed the rate rising and then falling as the free energy change became more negative, showing that the inverted region is real. Marcus was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1992 for this work.

prompt: Electron transfer between [Co(bpy)3]^{n+} complexes is fast for the Co(I)/Co(II) pair (k ≈ 10^9 M^−1 s^−1) but slow for the Co(II)/Co(III) pair (k = 18 M^−1 s^−1). Why?

choices.text: Co(II) is high spin and Co(III) is low spin, so the Co(II)/Co(III) transfer also requires electrons to shuffle between d orbitals on the same metal
Co(II) is low spin and Co(III) is high spin, so their bond lengths match
choices.why: The spin states are the other way around: low-charge Co(I) and Co(II) are expected to be high spin, and Co(III) is usually low spin.

choices.text: The Co(II)/Co(III) pair has a very large driving force, which puts it in the Marcus inverted region
choices.why: Transfer between Co(II) and Co(III) forms the same kinds of complexes, so there is no large driving force. The problem is the spin change.

choices.text: The Co(III) complex is tetrahedral, while the others are octahedral
choices.why: All these complexes are octahedral, since bpy is a bidentate ligand.

explanation: All three complexes are octahedral. Co(I) and Co(II), with relatively low charge, are expected to be high spin, while Co(III) is usually low spin. In a transfer between Co(II) and Co(III), not only does one electron move from one metal to the other, but additional electrons have to shuffle between orbitals on the same metal to accommodate the change between high and low spin. That reorganization has a barrier, which slows the reaction.

prompt: In a flash photolysis study, electron transfer from Os(II) to Ru(III) is very fast (k_obs > 5 × 10^9 s^−1), but from Os(II) to Co(III) it is much slower (k_obs = 1.9 × 10^5 s^−1). What explains the difference?

choices.text: Os(II) and Ru(III) are both low spin and need no electronic reorganization, while Co(III) changes from low spin to high spin when it is reduced
Co(III) is high spin, while Os(II) is low spin, so electrons can't pass between them
choices.why: Co(III) starts out low spin. Its change to high-spin Co(II) after reduction adds a barrier, slowing the reaction but not stopping it.

choices.text: Ru(III) changes from low spin to high spin when reduced, which lowers the barrier
choices.why: Ru stays low spin, and a spin change raises the barrier rather than lowering it.

choices.text: Os(II) must change from low spin to high spin when it is oxidized
choices.why: Os(II) and Ru(III) are both low spin to begin with and need no reorganization. Only cobalt changes spin state.

explanation: Electron transfer between Os(II) and Ru(III) involves no electron reorganization, because both are low spin to begin with. Transfer from Os(II) to Co(III) turns low-spin cobalt into high-spin Co(II), so electrons must move between different d orbitals on the cobalt. That adds to the barrier and slows the reaction by more than four orders of magnitude.

prompt: Low-spin octahedral Co(III), a d^6 ion, has all six d electrons in t2g. When it gains an electron and becomes high-spin octahedral Co(II), a d^7 ion, how many electrons are in the eg level?
explanation: High-spin d^7 is t2g^5 eg^2, so 2 electrons are in eg. Going from low-spin Co(III) (t2g^6 eg^0) to high-spin Co(II), the added electron goes into eg and another electron must move from t2g to eg. This internal electronic reorganization adds to the barrier, which is why transfers that switch cobalt between low and high spin are slow.

prompt: Cr^2+ reduces [Co(NH3)6]^3+ with k = 10^−4 M^−1 s^−1, but reduces [Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+ with k = 6 × 10^5 M^−1 s^−1. By what factor does replacing one NH3 with Cl^− speed up the reaction?
explanation: (6 × 10^5) ÷ (10^−4) = 6 × 10^9. The chloride complex reacts about six billion times faster, and the chloride ends up on chromium as CrCl^2+. Both observations fit the chloride bridging the two metals: inner-sphere electron transfer.

prompt: When Cr^2+ reduces [Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+, the products are Co^2+, CrCl^2+ and 5 NH3 (aqua ligands omitted). What does the transfer of the chloride to chromium suggest?

choices.text: The chloride bridged the two metals, binding chromium with one of its additional lone pairs, and the electron transferred through this shared ligand
The electron transferred by an outer-sphere path, and the chloride was simply lost to solution
choices.why: The chloride is not lost: it ends up on chromium. Together with the huge rate increase, that points to a bridge between the metals.

choices.text: The chloride was oxidized to chlorine during the reaction
choices.why: Chloride stays chloride. Cobalt is reduced from Co(III) to Co(II), and chromium is oxidized from Cr(II) to Cr(III).

choices.text: Cobalt(II) binds chloride more strongly than chromium(III) does
choices.why: It's the other way around: the high-spin Co(II) product is labile, while the inert d^3 Cr(III) product holds on to the chloride.

explanation: The chloride reaction is much faster than the hexaammine reaction, and the chloride is transferred to chromium; the two observations are probably part of the same phenomenon. Chloride can use an additional lone pair to bind Cr^2+, so it is bound to both metals at once and forms a bridge between them. Afterward it remains on the chromium. Electron transfers that occur via ligands shared by the two metals are inner-sphere transfers.

prompt: After the inner-sphere reaction of [Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+ with Cr^2+, the chloride stays on chromium in CrCl^2+ because the chromium(III) product is inert. How many d electrons does Cr(III) have?
explanation: Chromium is in group 6, so it has 6 valence electrons; removing 3 leaves Cr^3+ as d^3. The d^3 Cr(III) complex is inert and keeps the chloride. The cobalt product, high-spin Co(II), is labile, so its ammonia ligands are easily replaced by water.

prompt: Which of these ligands could NOT serve as the bridge in an inner-sphere electron transfer?

choices.text: NH3
Oxalate
choices.why: Oxalate is one of the bridging ligands the section lists. After binding one metal, it still has lone pairs to bind a second.

choices.text: Azide
choices.why: Azide is listed as an inner-sphere bridge. It has additional lone pairs with which to bind a second metal ion.

choices.text: Thiocyanate
choices.why: Thiocyanate can bind one metal through S and the other through N, so it bridges well.

explanation: A bridging ligand must bind both metals at once, so after coordinating to one metal it needs an additional lone pair for the second. Halides, carboxylates, oxalate, azide, thiocyanate and pyrazine all qualify. Ammonia's only lone pair is used to bind its metal, so it has none left to form a bridge.

prompt: In water, [Fe(OH2)6]^2+ + [(SCN)Co(NH3)5]^2+ → [(NCS)Fe(OH2)5]^2+ + [Co(OH2)6]^2+ + 5 NH3. Thiocyanate starts bound to cobalt through S and ends bound to iron through N. What does this indicate?

choices.text: Thiocyanate bridged the two metals, and an electron passed from Fe(II) to Co(III) by an inner-sphere path
An electron passed from Co(III) to Fe(II) through the thiocyanate bridge
choices.why: Electrons flow from the reductant to the oxidant. Iron ends up as Fe(III) and cobalt as Co(II), so the electron moved from iron to cobalt.

choices.text: An electron passed from Fe(II) to Co(III) by an outer-sphere path
choices.why: Thiocyanate moving from cobalt to iron shows that it was shared by both metals, which makes the transfer inner-sphere.

choices.text: Cobalt was oxidized and lost its ammonia ligands
choices.why: Cobalt is reduced to Co(II), which is labile and exchanges its ammonia for water.

explanation: Thiocyanate has lone pairs on both S and N, so it can bind Co(III) through S and Fe(II) through N at the same time. The electron moves from Fe(II) to Co(III) across this bridge. Afterward, the thiocyanate stays on the new Fe(III), bound through N, while the reduced cobalt loses its ammonia ligands to water.

prompt: Once a chloride bridge links two metals, the electron can cross it by a "hole" mechanism. What happens in that mechanism?

choices.text: The chloride first donates an electron from one of its lone pairs to the metal being reduced, and the hole it leaves is then filled by an electron from the other metal
The reducing metal first puts an electron onto the chloride, which then passes it to the other metal
choices.why: That is the electron-migration mechanism, the alternative. For chloride it is unsatisfactory, because chlorine already has a full octet.

choices.text: The chloride dissociates and carries the electron through the solution
choices.why: In both bridge mechanisms the chloride stays bound to the two metals while the electron crosses.

choices.text: The two metals bond directly to each other and the chloride is not involved
choices.why: The electron crosses via the bridging chloride; the hole is created on the chloride itself.

explanation: In the hole mechanism, the bridging chloride donates one electron from an idle lone pair to the metal being reduced, leaving behind a "hole". The hole is then filled with an electron donated from the other metal. The alternative, electron migration from metal to bridge first, is unsatisfactory for chloride, which already has a full octet, but bridging ligands with low-lying unoccupied molecular orbitals could temporarily hold the extra electron.

prompt: Isied studied electron transfer between metal centers linked by polyproline bridges. Why is an inner-sphere pathway through such a bridge expected to be somewhat slow?

choices.text: The bridge lacks conjugation, with few π bonds or lone pairs to carry an electron or a hole along it
The bridge is so flexible that the metal–metal distance keeps changing
choices.why: Proline rings add conformational rigidity, which is why the distance increases steadily with each repeat unit.

choices.text: Conjugated bridges slow inner-sphere transfer, and polyproline is highly conjugated
choices.why: This is reversed. Conjugation helps inner-sphere transfer, and polyproline lacks it.

choices.text: Polyproline cannot bind to either metal
choices.why: Polyproline is the bridging ligand here. The problem is the lack of conjugation to shuttle electrons, not binding.

explanation: Although the ligand bridges the two metals, it is hard to picture either an electron or a hole mechanism through it: there are few π bonds or lone pairs where electrons could be temporarily placed or removed as they are shuttled along. A conjugated system would be much more likely to carry out inner-sphere electron transfer.

prompt: In Isied's polyproline-bridged complexes, k_obs is 5 × 10^8 s^−1 when the metal centers are 12.2 Å apart (n = 1) and 1.6 × 10^7 s^−1 when they are 14.8 Å apart (n = 2). By what factor does the rate constant drop on going from n = 1 to n = 2?
explanation: (5 × 10^8) ÷ (1.6 × 10^7) ≈ 31. Increasing the separation by 2.6 Å slows the transfer about thirtyfold. Over the whole series, though, a plot of log k against distance is not linear: it looks like two lines that cross, a classic symptom of two competing pathways.

prompt: Intramolecular electron transfer (within one molecule) can be contaminated by intermolecular transfer (between molecules). Which experiment does the section suggest to check that a measured rate is intramolecular?

choices.text: Measure the rate at a series of dilutions: intramolecular transfer is unaffected, while intermolecular transfer slows down
Measure the rate at a series of dilutions: intramolecular transfer slows down, while intermolecular transfer is unaffected
choices.why: This is reversed. Dilution moves molecules farther apart, slowing intermolecular transfer, but it can't change distances within one molecule.

choices.text: Raise the concentration so the molecules collide more often
choices.why: Higher concentration encourages the unwanted intermolecular transfer. Low concentration keeps molecules apart.

choices.text: Switch to a less polar solvent
choices.why: A less polar solvent would affect the barrier for any electron transfer, so it can't tell the two pathways apart.

explanation: Keeping the concentration low increases the distance between molecules and reduces the likelihood of intermolecular, outer-sphere transfer. Running the experiment at a series of dilutions tests this: intramolecular electron transfer is unaffected, while intermolecular transfer slows down. If the rates are the same across several concentrations, the reaction is probably intramolecular.
